utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Can everybody hear me? As regards the organisation of our work today, at 2.30 when we resume working, we will have a Status Conference, 2.30. All right, Judge Shahabuddeen, 2.30? The Judge was made aware of our discussions the day before yesterday, and so we will hear your observations, but we will discuss things, that is, discuss the situation in closed session, but this morning, we can hear the Defence witness testimony. Mr. Nobilo, are you going to be conducting the examination-in-chief? If I've understood correctly, there are no specific protective measures for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He did not ask for protective measures, and I will be conducting the examination. Mr. President, I have a request to make, first of all. We didn't work yesterday, and on two occasions, we're quite obviously going to devote some time, very usefully and importantly I might add, to the Status Conference, so that the time for listening to witness testimony has been reduced. We, in The Hague this week, have five new witnesses which have not been heard yet. I'm going to try and be as brief as possible and to focus on the essence with each witness, but may we retain this balance so that the cross-examination be equal in the time span to the examination-in-chief. We're going to speak of events and not of the chain of command. We're going to speak of events that took place in their villages, and if we were to focus our work on this, we might be able to get through by Friday at 1.00 p.m., as you know, Monday is a holiday, and so the costs would be increased disproportionately. So could we try to do this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleague on a point. Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. The Judges' answer was the following: The time for the cross-examination in principle will be exactly the same as the time of the examination-in-chief, nonetheless, with a degree of flexibility with the Prosecution being responsible for demonstrating that he needs more time. Do we agree? In other words, let me repeat myself. The time that will be given to the Prosecutor for his cross-examination, in principle -- in principle, I repeat -- will be exactly the same, that is, cannot exceed the amount of time that the examination-in-chief takes. However, the Judges would like to introduce the notion of flexibility and, therefore, depending on the witness, the Prosecutor will have to tell the Judges that he needs more time, and the Judges will make the evaluation. But in principle, the cross-examination will be the same amount of time as the examination-in-chief for all of the witnesses, all the way through the end of next week, that is, all of the witnesses being heard pursuant to Rule 71. Having said this, Mr. Nobilo, please have your witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. This witness will take the longest time, an hour and a half, I suppose, for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, sir? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing for a moment. Tell us your name, your first name, the date and place of your birth, your profession, and your current residence, and after that, you will take an oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Marijan Strukar. I was born on the 6th of May, 1956 in Travnik. I now reside in Vitez, and I work in the insurance company there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You can now take the oath by reading the statement that's being given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. You have agreed to come to testify at the request of the Defence in the trial which has been initiated against General Blaskic who, at the time of the events, was a Colonel. You will answer Mr. Nobilo's questions and then the Prosecutor's questions and then, perhaps, the Judges' questions. Mr. Nobilo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, you've already told the Court that you were born in Travnik in 1956. Can you tell us where you went to school, what schools you have completed, and what you did before the war conflicts broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I was born in Travnik, I was just born there, but immediately after my birth, I went to Vitez where I went to primary school. After that, I completed a secondary mechanics school in Novi Travnik, and having completed that school, I went to work in the Unis factories in Vitez. The factory's name is Vitezit, and I worked in the maintenance department and was later head of production, head of the production unit and department, for the packaging of plastic explosives. This is a department which was composed of a printing department, cartoning, and a mechanics unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you lived in Vitez. Could you describe where your house was located, and then you can point it out to us on the diagram that you have drawn for us.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: My house in Vitez, and we in Vitez call the section where my house was located upper Vitez, Gornji Vitez, it was some 200 metres before you come to the Catholic church on the other side of the road, which means approximately 200 metres from the Mahala, that is to say, between the church and the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we define this by saying that your house was what was later to become the frontline between the Muslim forces and the Croat forces in Vitez, between the Mahala and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. That was that particular locality. That was where the delineation ran, the frontline, from my house to that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now take a look at the diagram. Could you tell us who drew up the diagram and what it represents to help us become better oriented, where the Mahala house is, where your house is, and where the church is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I, myself, drew up this diagram to be able to recall where the houses stood, the houses that existed before the beginning of the conflict. On the diagram, I have included the Croat houses and the Muslim houses, all of them, and the coloured ones are the ones that were burnt in the first days of the conflict. May I get up to indicate this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, and would you please explain the symbols you used to denote the Croat houses and the Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This is my house here (indicating), and the Muslim houses I have marked in the following way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you use this colour for your own house and place an arrow, please, by your house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: (Marks). That is my house or the place where my house was located on the diagram. This is the Catholic church up here (indicating). Down here is the part that we referred to as the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. For purposes of the record, you have used an orange marker and have placed an arrow to designate your own house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Next on the diagram, for purposes of clarification, I have marked all the Muslim houses, houses owned by the Muslims, with squares, whereas the Croatian houses owned by Croats, I denoted with triangles. The others are denoted with squares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I have a visual problem because the projector is in my way. No, no, it's not necessary to move it. Perhaps Mr. Nobilo can ask the witness to be a little clearer as to the location of his house in relation, A, to the Catholic church, and, B, to the Mahala. I may have missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you indicate your house once more, but keep the pointer by your house so that the interpretation can catch up with you, so don't move the pointer away from your house for a little while. And, secondly, could you mark the arrow a little more clearly because I can't see it very well, let alone the Judges. Now, try and indicate your house once again, please, to us.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This is my house here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where is the Catholic church? Point that out to us now, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This is the street (indicating). At the upper end lies the Catholic church, so this is the street, going straight down here (indicating), and this is where the Mahala starts, what we referred to as the Mahala. So my house is somewhere midway between the Mahala and the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll leave the diagram up on the board for a moment, but I'd like Mr. Dubuisson to assign a number for that diagram because we shall tender it as evidence. Let me now ask you, a week before the conflict in Vitez broke out, which broke out on the 16th of April, 1993, were you employed? Were you working at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I was employed at the time because my employment did not stop, although in the last couple of months prior to the beginning of the war, there was not enough work for all the employees to do, so that in my department, for example, and that was what happened in all the other departments, we only had the absolute minimum number of workers necessary to perform the tasks that were there to be done, which means that our work had dropped to about 20 per cent of what it usually was, so we went to work for awhile and then went back, and we, in fact, referred to this as waiting. We were waiting for work to turn up for us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you said that you were at home during this period?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Any Muslim or any Croat, were they fired from the factory in Vitez at the time, any single Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You mean by some other force?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that they were fired, relieved of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No. I don't know of any single case like that. All of us, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims, there were some others as well, nobody lost their job at that time. We were just waiting, and when our time came up, we would spend, that is to say, 15 or 20 days at home, and then we would be called to come to work when there was work for us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the eve of the conflict, the 15th of April, 1993, and prior to that, were you a soldier? What was your status at the time? Could you explain this for the benefit of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, where I live, there were very few soldiers, I did not know any, actually, very few, and as far as I, myself, am concerned, for 20 years before the war broke out, I was a member of the voluntary fire brigade unit, and in the last five or six years, I was chief of that fire brigade unit, so that sometime in the autumn of 1992, I received my mobilisation call-up from the Territorial Defence and the Croatian Defence Council. We received joint invitations for mobilisation into the unit for fire protection for the whole town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like these two requests for call-up to be handed out. We have copies, so would you assign numbers to them, please, and hand them out?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: While we're preparing these call-up papers, could you tell us, please, whether your unit was a Croat fire brigade unit, a Muslim one, or a mixed one?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, principally, it was mixed, a mixed unit, because it was composed of individuals who wished, on a voluntary basis, to work in the fire brigade without receiving remuneration for it, so there were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims making up the fire brigade. And the people that did this kind of work were called up and invited to take up their duties in that unit because of what was going on in Croatia and in certain areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, this multi-national unit, how long did it remain multi-national?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That unit remained multi-national practically to the very last night before the conflict, yes, that's right, to the eve of the conflict, and the last duty shift that was done was done by a Croat, a Serb, and a Muslim. They all took part in that last shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have these two call-up invitations, unfortunately, only in Croatian, because we have received them from the witness, so I would like to read them out. The first is from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Which numbers have been assigned to these documents, please? Could you tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the map, this would be D513. For the first document where the date is on the upper left-hand corner, that's D514, and then the next one would be D515.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, could we define this document, whether it is a BH army document or a Croatian Defence Council document and the dates.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All right. D515 is the one which has on the upper left-hand corner "Armija BH."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am, first of all, going to read out document D515, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the BH army, the headquarters in Vitez, a call-up paper for service in the BH army, for mechanic Marijan Vladimira Strukar, born in 1956 in Vitez, and the other things that are stated are the street, the street number, the telephone number, and the place of employment have been left blank. "To report, on the 23rd of November, 1992 immediately upon receiving the call-up papers to report to the unit," and it says, "CZ," "civilian protection," that is, civilian defence, "and the fire brigade, to report to the fire brigade headquarters," and it is signed and stamped, and the signature is barely visible. The second document, D514, in the memorandum, we have "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council," that is the heading, "Vitez." The number is referred to as "SL." The date is the 23rd of November, 1992, and it is a call-up for Strukar, Vladimira Marijan; date of birth, the 6th of May, 1956; rank has been left void; ves, void again; residing in Vitez. The municipality is left blank; street, blank; street number, blank; telephone number, blank; place of employment/company, blank. "To report immediately upon reception of these call-up papers to the headquarters for civil defence, the fire brigade. The locality to be reported to, the fire brigade centre in Vitez. Representative for defence is Dragan Strbac," as far as I can see, signed and stamped, and the little letters below the line states that if the individual fails to comply with the call-up papers and report, that they will be responsible in keeping with disciplinary action that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is entitled to take. Therefore, Mr. Strukar, are these photocopies an authentic representation of the call-up papers you received on or around the 23rd of November, 1992, the documents that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, these are authentic representations. The originals are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your headquarters were in the fire brigade centre. Is that not where the Bosniak, it was called the Muslim police at the time for Vitez, and the Territorial Defence headquarters were, that is to say, the army? So could you explain to us what this was like? Did you have any problems with the members of the army and police of the Muslims in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In addition to the fire brigade building, which was there for years, at least 20 years, I think, at any rate, for as long as I had been a fireman, there are apartments upstairs, and downstairs, there are some shops. And at that time, when they were looking for premises, how should I put this, then some members of the Muslim forces took these premises, the offices and shops downstairs, so that that is where their police was. Some of them were the civilian police, some of them were the military police, I don't know, so it was that building that I just described that leaned against the building of the fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: However, all these armed formations, either civilian or military, belonged to the Bosniak people in Vitez; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I said. These were Muslim police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, were there any conflicts or incidents with your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. There were a few incidents. I would like to specifically mention one where I was involved and the fire brigade. One day, I cannot give you the exact date, but that is the day when the bank caught on fire and we went to try to extinguish the fire, my firemen did, not me, because I couldn't make it. And these firemen of mine, they were taken prisoner by these Muslim policemen. I don't know if it is necessary for me to go into all of this, but they got out with rifles, and they sent them all back to the garage, the men and the vehicles, everybody and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there another incident near the shop of Nikola Krizanac who is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was another incident. I would like to show this to you on this diagram, to show you where this shop is. So if this is my house, the shop I mentioned is here (indicating), and the fire brigade building is 200 or 300 metres away from this shop, but it's not here on the diagram, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. We have a transcript, you see, so, of course, they cannot visually depict everything that you're saying. So your house is marked with an orange arrow; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And Nikola Krizanac or, rather, his house is marked by a triangle which is half red, and the third building along the road going down from the bottom, from Stari Vitez, the third one there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So now could we hear your description of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. The fire brigade building that we discussed is down the road, as we would put it, about 200 or 300 metres away from the shop I mentioned. I don't know until the present day why, but the police obviously had received some kind of a report stating that something went wrong, and they came with their men and weapons. They went to that shop, and they stopped a cistern of the public utilities company, and they stopped it on the road, and this took all afternoon and all night. At that time, there simply was no traffic from the direction of my house and the fire brigade building. However, since my house is nearby, during the night, naturally, I was afraid, and I was wondering what was going on, and I had to keep watching to see what was going on, and during the night, I saw this shop being looted. I phoned my own men at the fire brigade building where there were some Muslims too, and I told them, "Tell the commanders that the young men who are there are looting the shop and that they're nervous."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who's nervous, the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, up there, my Croat neighbours, they saw this too, and this was the situation where there was no shooting and everything, and you don't know what to do, and you see that things are being carried out of the shop. So I informed my colleague from the fire brigade to -- I asked him to talk to the commander there, and he said that he had told him; however, in the morning, when all of this was over, the shop was empty. There was nothing left in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us call this a military exercise of taking positions vis-a-vis the Croats. When did this happen? Can you remember, at least, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I really could not tell you the exact date, but it was sometime before the new year of 1992, but I can't remember exactly. Sorry, I said '92. I'm actually referring to December '92, but it was supposed to be the new year of 1993. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now let us move on to the event that you are actually supposed to testify about. The conflict in Vitez broke out on the 16th of April, 1993. Could you please explain about the 15th of April, the day preceding the 16th? When did you become aware of the fact that something was going on which will later on be linked up to the events of the 16th of April and onwards?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In order for me to answer the lawyer's question, I have to tell you that as soon as the war broke out in Croatia and in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had self-imposed, so to speak, some kind of guard duty around our houses. We did this during the night. These were groups of people who would not go to sleep, and together -- and we didn't do this together with the Muslims. For some reason, we guarded our own houses, the Muslims guarded their own houses, and we took turns, and sometimes there wasn't any guard duty at all when, I don't know, somebody would phone someone and say that the situation was normal. So at that time, on the eve of the 16th, there was no guard duty of this nature, so it was supposed to be some kind of a safe situation. Sometime around 7.30 p.m., a friend of mine came --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You're talking about the 15th of April; right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the 15th of April. I'm talking about 7.30 p.m., approximately. A friend came and said -- well, I cannot give you his exact words, but approximately, he said, "The Muslims are preparing something again. It would be a good thing for you to come so that we could see what to do." I was not really surprised because this had happened before, as I already said. So I went up there towards the Catholic church, and in front of the church, there is a square where, from our childhood days, we would gather and talk and we would play as children. Can I show this on the map? It's over here (indicating). It's this square up here. When I came up there it -- there were already some 15 or 20 neighbours of mine who had already come and who had no idea what was going on. Of course, we thought that we should have this kind of guard duty again, to take care of our houses. But since nothing was happening, and we didn't know anything, somebody had received some kind of information and said, "Nothing doing. Perhaps it would be a good thing, nevertheless, for someone to remain on guard duty afterall." And we could not really reach agreement on this. And we said, "Well, how about all of those who are sleepy, going home to sleep, and those who were not sleepy would stay up and patrol," and then they could wake us up later when they were fed up. I was one of the lucky ones who went home, and I went back home -- I usually go to bed late. I sat and talked to my wife for quite some time. My children went to sleep. However, around 11.30 or 12.00 a friend of mine said it would be a good idea if you went out because something seems to be amiss. I didn't want to worry my wife because there were sort of alarms of this kind on several occasions and, when I went up there and came to the square again, I found that there was a group of people there once again, and once again they didn't know anything. But something was felt in the air, that something was wrong. One could feel that something was wrong. And when there were more serious threats and alarms, so-to-speak, those of us who lived nearer to the Mahala, that is to say all these houses here to which I am indicating on the diagram, during these alarms, would take their wives and children and take them away to some of the houses that were situated further away from the Mahala. And as we were not certain what was actually going on, they cautioned me and said that I should wake up my wife and go to a place of greater safety, because, based on the experience of the war in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was usually the civilians closest to the areas where a conflict started were usually the ones to suffer. So that's what I did. I woke my wife up and then the children and I said, "Let's go and look for safety." I took them where there -- and as my parents live in the house next door to me, and I'll indicate this once again on the diagram here. I have my mother and father, my sister and her child. They were all living in the next door house. And so I took them to the house of Nikola Banic, and that's this house up there. Then I went back to fetch my parents. But my father, like all fathers, said, "I don't want to take part in these war games of yours. You've done this to me several times before. I am not going." But I managed to convince my mother and my sister and her son to leave the house. And all of this took place by 3.00 a.m. or 3.30 a.m., and some of my close neighbours also moved their families out. And then nothing happened. And the men folk, that is to say we men who were expected to be able to tell their families what was going on, and in fact where my family was being put up, some 20 other people were there. But we didn't know anything. We just got information that the Muslims were preparing something, but we actually know what. So we would just stay around the house or smoke outside. And all of this lasted up until dawn. It was still dark, though. And we tried to get more information. I remember that someone at one point said, "You shouldn't worry any more," because we were worried for their families and their safety. And somebody said, "You needn't worry because some young men from Nova Bila have arrived." Nova Bila is by Travnik. And they came and said that we shouldn't be frightened. They said that they were experienced fighters and that they would protect them. And we talked about this, but you could feel the nervousness, it was tangible, and expecting somebody in uniform to turn up armed. And so as people were nervous, someone came and saw us sitting in front of the house and sort of moaning, and they said -- he said, "Now, what are you doing here? Leave that place. Go back down to your houses." So that we were moving around. Can I show this on the diagram? So we moved from this house where my family was situated, we went down this road from Ivica Blaz's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So on the map those of the Croatian houses are in the upper right-hand corner of the diagram, and they have been designated with a triangle?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. So we were moving around in this area up here. And that's what happened in the course of that particular night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did everything start? Could you describe that to us?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Sometime around dawn, it was already dawn but not enough light yet, we heard a strong explosion. Up until then there had been small scale explosions in Vitez. Some young boys were playing around with bombs. But this was a stronger explosion, stronger than the ones we had previously heard. Now, I am not a professional in warfare or for explosives, but I do know that some form of lightening from the explosion could be heard, and the detonation was audible from where we were somewhere here. And it came across the Lasva River, from across the Lasva River. At the time there were no settlements there, there was just a petrol station and perhaps one house. But I am certain that's where the explosion came from. And we did not know what this was all about. And there was silence for two or three minutes after that explosion. Then we heard sporadic gunfire and, once again, silence reigned. However, at that particular moment we heard shooting from this point here, and it was coming from the street. It was coming from the street in which we were located. I don't know what actually happened. We were afraid. We didn't know who was shooting, who was being shot at, why. This lasted some ten minutes, the shooting lasted for about ten minutes, and then some of us rushed up to their families who were put up in the houses over there to protect them. When I approached the house, that is to say when I went from Nikola Banic, that is in the right-hand corner, yes, where my family was located, families were arriving, some Muslim families were arriving, men, women and children. And the young men from Bila expelled them from their own houses and sent them to the houses where our civilians were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "our civilians," you mean the Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. I am thinking of my own family principally because my family was there and two other families and the inhabitants of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there serious shooting in that part of Vitez at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: For me I would say that it was serious shooting, because we heard shots, we heard shooting from rifles. I heard that particular sound. And then afterwards something stronger could be heard in the course of the day. For example, a gun -- a cannon was heard. It was on a truck, on a flatbed truck. It is an anti-aircraft gun with 20 millimetre barrels, three barrels of 20 millimetres, and in the houses where we were located, as far as I could see, rifle grenade and rifle grenades were being seen and shot. So they hit the roofs, exploded and dropped into the yards. So there was shooting of this kind from the rifle grenade launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What were you able to conclude? Where were these rifle grenades coming from?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, these shells were coming from the direction of the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear the whistle of bullets? Did you hear shooting from the Mahala from small arms as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, we were protected by the houses in front of us, but there were bullets that hit the tiles of the roofs and, as I say, the rifle grenades which hit the roofs and reverberated and fell into the yards where we were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened next? You were with your father, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. I had taken my mother and sister up to the houses up there, but my father didn't want to leave. So this was an anxiety for me. But I didn't go any further because from the upper half, which -- the upper half of the street we could see smoke coming from that side, that is to say across the street. The side of the road opposite my house I could see flames and smoke and the Muslims coming from there were crying and saying that their houses had been set on fire. So that the shooting and the explosion and the houses on fire all led to great fear. I was afraid, more than being afraid for my father and his life. So I was very worried about my own house as well, what had happened to it, because it was set fire to as well. And I consulted with my colleagues and asked them what I should do, and a friend of mine, his name is Mlakic, Darko Mlakic, and he lives in a house in front of mine, towards the Mahala, and said that his father had also stayed in his house because he was a diabetic, and that his brother had remained to look after the father, who was not able to stay on his own. So we decided to go down, because there -- we decided to go and see what had happened to our parents. I remember that on several occasions we tried to leave, but we were not experienced fighters, that is to say we were no fighters at all, and we were very much afraid. And we would move forward a couple of metres or ten metres and then were so frightened that we would rush back, because there were bullets being fired all around. And then we felt ashamed, of course, for not being braver. And we had our sort of male pride, which made us go out again. And then the friend in whose house we were located was a huntsman and he said it would be a good idea to take one of the rifles. And he convinced us to do so, and he gave us his hunting rifle with two barrels and two bullets. And I took this rifle and then we went to move downwards with the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many bullets did you have, actually?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Had you two bullets?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about your colleague, the one that went with you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: He had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This probably sounds strange to you, but this shotgun bothered us more than it helped us, because they were really talking us into it. So the two of us went back and went out again, but we went between these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this is on the side of the road that is closer to the Lasva River; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's where my house is and where Darko's house is. We were hiding behind houses, like, you know, what you see on television. And at one moment we realised that quite a bit of time had gone by and we did manage to reach my house and my father's house, and we found my father in the basement of the house. He did go downstairs afterall, although he had stayed in the house. And, of course, I was happy to see that he was alive. However, he said something like, "What is this? What's going on?" And I remember telling him, "Well, at least people are alive." Because until then I had seen all my Croat neighbours, all the Croats, all the Muslims, they were all alive and all of them were in two or three houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please turn to the Judges when you answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. All these civilians who were there, our neighbours, Muslims and Croats, they were all staying at these houses, and I know that nobody was killed. And I thought, well -- but it was very difficult for me to see the houses on fire because for so many years I had belonged to the fire brigade. And then my father told me, "What do you mean there are no people who are killed? Look at the dead in front of the house." And I asked who, and then he said, "Our neighbour Becko."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Sadibasic is his name, but I remember from the moment he was born, everybody called him Becko. And I said, "Where is he?" He said he was right in front of the house. Since we were in the basement and the basement had a door facing the Mahala and our neighbour Sulejman's door, I peeked through this door and I saw Becko lying in the street, and of course later on I realised that he was dead. Naturally, Darko and I were horrified by this. This was a friend of ours. And until then I had thought that there were no people who were killed or wounded. But then after that my father added that as he went downstairs, he saw that Ejud Sadibasic had been killed and the son of this man Sulejman and also some refugees from Jajce near Salid's house. I tried to talk my father into going back then. I was simply afraid. And I had the feeling that these people who were up there should be told what was going on, because my father didn't want to stay in the basement, but Darko and I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before you describe how you went back, would you tell us whether there were any problems with your car. What had happened to your car and how had it disappeared from your house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: During this explanation, while my father was telling me about our neighbour Sulejman, that he was killed, I said, "Well, how did this happen?" And he said, "I don't know." But also a boy from Nova Bila was killed too. And then in front of my father's house is the garage where my car is. And he said that he had been wounded there, but actually he had already been dead, and they just thought that he was wounded. And he said that they -- that "He was hit there and they took your car," he said, "to take them to the hospital." I saw that the door, the garage door was ajar, but I didn't really think of going near the garage at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now we are going to stop the chronological sequence of events. So could you please just tell the Court at this point what you heard later and from whom; how Becko was killed, his son and this HVO soldier from Nova Bila, how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: At that moment, that is to say when I saw Sulejman, I just knew what my father had told me, but naturally one always tries to find out what had actually happened. So two or three days later I talked to another next door neighbour of mine, but the one who actually lived across the street from me. I am going to show it to you on the map. He lives in this house. Pero Milosevic is the owner's name. He's a Serb, if that's important. And that morning, when there was this shooting and when the houses were on fire and he, poor man, did not know what was going on, because no one called him, the Muslims or the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean the --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, the house is a bit high up and it's rather dominant, so from his window he could see what was going on. He saw these men in uniform, who were running up and down the road, and at one moment he saw -- it's not of course that he could really look through the window. He was standing a bit further back from the window. He saw Sulejman's oldest son, that is the Sulejman I was telling you about who was lying dead in the road, these young men who were coming from Nova Bila. He ran out of the house with a gun and -- I am talking about this house, Sulejman Sadibasic's house. The door is on this side. And he ran out with a rifle and he was running down here below the house. There's a small stream down here. Then he went behind the house and then there was natural shelter here between the fences. And that's where he put his rifle. And then he started shooting at these young men from Nova Bila, and practically there between his house and mine he killed this man from Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, before we proceed. Let us try to clarify this. Sulejman Sadibasic, who were killed, and his son and his sons are Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please proceed now and tell us what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I am telling you about everything that Pero Milosevic had told me. So this oldest son of Sulejman Sadibasic, I think his name was Safet, he was shooting and he hit this young man from Nova Bila. And that's when all the shooting really started that actually killed all these people. I did not mention that before all of this had happened we were all neighbours there. We all speak the same language. And these young men who came in, they had some kind of white bands on their arms. And that is how we distinguished between themselves and us. And, actually, so these men were shooting at all these people who did not have these arm bands. So that is when Sulejman was killed and Ejub Sadibasic and Sulejman's son and another man from Jajce, I don't know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: According to this Milosevic's story, could you use a green magic marker to show where Sadibasic and his sons were killed, and could you use a red marker to show where, according to this story, the soldier from Nova Bila was killed. If you can do this, please do, and I am going to give you the magic markers. I'm sorry I didn't realise that we did not have a green marker. We have a blue one. So please show the blue marker to show the place -- my colleague has a green one, but I think this one is a stronger colour, so we are going to use it. Thank you all the same. So we are going to use the red pen for marking where the man from Nova Bila was killed and we are going to use the green one for showing the directions from which the HVO soldiers from Nova Bila were shooting. So you are going to show where the soldiers from Nova Bila, where those who were shooting. So first of all, where was -- yes. First use the blue pen to show where Sadibasic was killed, and these men, these Muslims whom you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: So now I am going to mark the place where I saw Sulejman lying, and after that where I saw his son and this other one. This is where I saw Sulejman Sadibasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you put in a circle. Could you please put in an even bigger circle, it's not really proportionate to the house, but that's not important. So -- yes. Yes. The blue circle represents the place where Sadibasic was. Please proceed. Where were the other Muslims killed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I said that on that day I only saw Sulejman where I saw him, but towards three days later they were still there because nobody could come up to them, but I didn't see it on that first day, but I found out later that his son, Sulejman's son, was killed here on this side. And also there was another body there too, around here. Actually, there were two over there. So I could not see that until later. But that's where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you now please use the red pen to mark a circle showing where you heard, according to the story you heard, that the Croat from Nova Bila was killed.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That's the place that my father described to me, because he had already been taken away in my car, and he was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now, please, would you use this green marker that we got through the kindness of our colleague, the Prosecutor, could you please draw lines to show the direction in which the other Croats were shooting after their colleague had been killed. Could you please use the green marker to show that.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It's quite difficult for me -- no, no, no, I am not having trouble with the pen. I mean I did not see these people when they were shooting. I just heard other people telling me about this. So they were somewhere around these other houses that are up there. But Pero told me where Safet had been, so I can only guess, since Safet was here, they were shooting from these houses, from the direction of these houses. Not from the houses, but from the direction of these houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object to this part of the testimony. This witness did not see this. He is guessing. Guesses cannot help the finders of fact, it appears to me, Mr. President, so I would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is telling us what an eyewitness had told him. Regrettably, the eyewitness had died and this is the only testimony that we can provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Nobilo. Mr. Harmon, the Judges consider that this is a relevant question and the Judges will make their evaluation. This is a very old discussion, that is the one having to do with hearsay, and it was brought up by the common law specialist, which includes, among others, Mr. Hayman. I think each of the parties has allowed each of the other's witnesses to speak when it has to do with things that they did not witness directly. Therefore, this is a relevant question which the Judges will be in a position to evaluate at the proper time. All right. Continue, Mr. Nobilo, and, Mr. Strukar, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please mark the directions with green arrows, that is to say the directions from which the men from Nova Bila were shooting when they actually shot these Muslims. So these are green arrows. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: According to the story I heard, it was supposed to be from this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now we are going to continue in chronological order, in terms of what you had seen yourself. So you were coming back from your father, he remained at your house or, rather, his house, and you were moving towards the Catholic church where there were more Croat houses. Could you please describe what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As I was going back, most of these houses that were marked by a red pen were already on fire. Bullets could be heard. At that time I felt that they were flying pretty low. Probably they were. Darko and I were running. We simply wanted to get there and to tell everybody what we had seen. Naturally, when we got there, since there were both Croats and Muslims there, we said that there were dead people there, and that there was a real war going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At one point in time did the young men from Nova Bila withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: After we told them this, they expected us to go back again, to go back down there, because Darko's father and Darko's brother were there too. And we were supposed to try and see whether they were still alive. However, as we were going back, the shooting had subsided. I don't know if you can really say subsided, but if you think of how intensive it was before that. I realised that a single bullet is shooting, so if somebody is shooting, even one bullet can do a lot of harm, but the shooting wasn't that intensive any more. I came across a young man over there near the house and I said, "What is going on now?" And he said, "Nothing. We ran out of ammunition." And I simply couldn't believe it. What kind of an answer was that. When I got down to my father, to my father's house, and as we started wondering how we could reach Zeljko Mlakic's house, all of a sudden these men had disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "these young men?" You are referring to the young men from Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the young men from Nova Bila who were around my house and these other houses. They simply -- they were nowhere to be seen. When I went back to those houses where there were civilians, they said they saw them get into cars and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time was it around 3.00? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a bit earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, in the afternoon of the 16th of April, what did the defence of Vitez look like on your side? Who defended the positions from the Lasva River to the road and who defended the positions on the other side of the street?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: At that moment, that is to say when these young men from Nova Bila left, on this side of the street where the Lasva River is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please show us this.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. This is the side where my house is too. We were there -- I mean, only my friend Darko and I, and our fathers were still in their respective houses. And we were wondering whether they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the only weapons you had were -- it was still the shotgun you told us about?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, the shotgun I told you about. We did not see anything happening on the other side, I am referring to the other side of the street, because we were not brave enough to call out anyone's name or to peek or whatever. But in the afternoon we did manage to see our neighbours who live on that side of the street, Ljuban Pavlovic with his son, Ivica Tihi, Zdravko Pavlovic, and then we managed to ask them about what had happened to the rest of the people there, and they said that they were on their own too. Ljuban Pavlovic, Ljuban Pavlovic was also a huntsman, so he had a shotgun too, a few of them. So they had some shotguns. And I asked, "What about your other neighbours?" And they said, "No one is there. Only our Muslim neighbours from these houses, they were in Ivan Tihi's house." I am showing you on the map now. I am showing you where this house is. So from them I found out that there were five of them there and the Muslims were hidden in the basement of this house, so that nothing would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the defence was as you described it. However, at one point, on the 16th of April, did you get some help afterall?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I must say that we were very worried, because that is not the way we had imagined a war to be, the kind of war that was raging all around us. I am referring to the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were terrified. These men from Nova Bila came in, they were shooting, they had set some houses on fire and they left. And we realised that our neighbours would feel that we were to blame for what had happened. And we wondered what to do. And we knew that the Muslims had weapons and they had their own police, et cetera, so we were wondering what would happen. However, at dusk, Darko Kraljevic came with his Vitezovi, and this is -- this is -- well, the first time I saw them because before that I had only heard of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If we were to summarise this day, the 16th, what is your experience? What did you understand? On the other side, on the Muslim side in the Mahala, is there some kind of a serious defence there, more meaningful than the one you had? What was your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That was my conclusion. These young men from Nova Bila who came and who were shooting to and fro, they were shooting at them and they were shooting back at them, when one of their own was killed, they withdrew because they tried to do some more. They wanted to go all the way up to the point where there were Croat houses, and they didn't manage to do that, and then they withdrew, and they realised that there was some kind of a line over there that was being held by someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The night between the 16th and 17th, was that a relatively peaceful night without any combat operations of any significance?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: During that night, I realised that it was quite a peaceful night or, rather, later I realised how peaceful the night had been. You could hear a bullet or two or a burst of gunfire or two, and then UNPROFOR tanks, I know that they were going up and down the road, so it was quite a night in terms of some of these events, but there was no fighting because the Vitezovi were somewhere up there near Vlasic facing the Serbs, so it didn't really mean anything for them. I mean, they'd just fire a burst of gunfire into the air and that was it, so it wasn't all that peaceful, but it wasn't bad either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, as the war went on further, the 17th, et cetera, what are the events that you particularly remember?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In order to explain that, I would have to go back to this night that was quite peaceful, as I said, that my friend and I had agreed to try to reach the house where his father was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, it's a rather long explanation. Perhaps we could take a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar, for having had the heat turned up here. Otherwise, all the Judges are going to get sick, then the lawyers, then the accused, and then the witnesses, and finally the interpreters. All right, we can resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We arrived at the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1993. You said you would like to add something to your description of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I was having a problem with my headset. Would you ask the question again, Mr. Nobilo, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I said that we had stopped with the events that took place in the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1993, but I had the feeling that the witness wanted to say something more on the events of the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, actually, I wanted to say something about that particular night and my conduct during that night. The night between the 16th and the 17th of April, I said that there was a lull and that the father of my friend who was with me was in the house in front of the frontline with his son because he was ill. The two of us had decided to try and reach the house to see whether he was alive. We saw that the house was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think he said, "not on fire."

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Having been hit by bullets and rifle grenades, and when it was quiet and we thought it was safe, we decided that we would go down by the lower end of the house, and I'll indicate that on the diagram. The two of us were here at my house (indicating), and his house was located here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that is on your side of the road. The triangle which is located behind the square house which was half burnt down has a mark within the square?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. We decided to go by this end where there were no houses, there was just a stream and some bushes, to try and reach the house to see if they were alive. I was a little more afraid because it was not my parent, actually, so I decided that I would stay behind and let him go in front. And when he reached the level of this house, which was half burnt down, he returned because he did not dare go on further. When he came back, he said he had noticed at a window of this half-burnt-down house a light, something that appeared to be a light.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you show us this house. This is Becko's house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, the one who was killed, and he was below this stream, the creek. And when he came back, he said that he felt that, although the house was in darkness, he saw a faint light coming through one of the windows, so he came back, he didn't dare go forward, and I justified this and told him that it was quite natural that he was afraid, and so he came back anyway. So this is an interesting event during that night. It would turn out to be something quite different afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us now move on towards the 17th of April. What do you remember about the 17th of April onwards, what events?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In the morning when it was dawn, shooting broke out again. I did not know who started the shooting, but there was shooting from both sides. The two of us were still there alone, and my father was there with us, and at one point, we did not even think of crossing the road because there was shooting along the road from both sides, and it would have been easy to have been killed there. But the commander of the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic, ran over to us to see what was happening. He was a little braver, so he ran across to us, and all we could say to him was that if he could, one of his men or he himself should try and reach the house of my friend to see whether his father and brother were still alive. He promised that he would try to do something, and he crossed the street again. He went to the opposite side of the street. After some time had elapsed, perhaps half an hour or one hour, he told us, calling to us across the road, that he had seen my friend's brother in the house, that he had called out to him, and he said that they were alive but that they were frightened to leave the house, and he said it was rather dangerous for them to return moving along our side of the road, but that he would do his best to pull them out of the house. We attended all this from my house and my father's house, and we later found that he would take out his father, and when he gave him the signal to cross the road, he would do so. So we watched all this, and at that time, Mario, with his mother, crossed the street, but the father was old and infirm, and he fell down in the middle of the road, and then heavy shooting began from both sides, and that was when -- it was like a film, and I saw for the first time one of Darko's Vitezovi rush out into the street and cover the two of them with his own body, sheltering the two, and went down towards the Mahala. Mario returned to collect up his father, and they crossed over and stayed alive, but that is an event that I remember very well to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At one point, your house was destroyed. Can you briefly describe to the Court how your house was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Probably on the second day --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We're going to see a video. There is no tone but we'll look at the video.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Probably on that second day when my friend came to my house and returned to where our families were located, at one point, we heard a strong explosion, and when we turned, we saw that there was smoke coming from the direction of my house. Something told me that it was my house, and I was very much afraid for my father's life, as he was still down there. We rushed back, and there was, indeed, smoke coming from my own house, and I saw that something had hit my house from the direction of the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that your house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's my house and the place where it was hit by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As there was smoke in the house and the walls were burning, and as I was a fireman by profession, I wanted to extinguish the fire, but I couldn't see anything for the smoke. I just tripped over something that was not usually there, not a usual shape, and when the smoke subsided, I saw that they were the remains of a grenade which was used in a multi-barrel rifle grenade launcher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps there is a coordination problem between what the witness is saying and the video or else have the witness comment on the video, but he has to comment about the pictures that we're seeing or else he should finish his narrative -- do you see what I mean, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I'd like to have the last picture on the video and have a still of it, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So let's move on from here. I'm going to ask you, and we can play the tape alongside this, whether here on the facade we can see traces of bullets that hit your house.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They are holes made by the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what's this?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This is part of the grenade that fell onto my house, and that was what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On that grenade or missile, did you see any markings and were you able to ascertain what type of weapon stormed your house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. There is the motor to the rocket, to this missile, it was a multiple rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that what it said on the remains of this grenade?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it says so on the lower part where the motor is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, the hole in the wall through which this grenade entered, where did it go towards?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It was turned towards the direction of the Mahala, that is to say, between my house and the Mahala is a meadow, a clearing, a clear space, and then you come to the house which was their defence line, in fact, so that there is a clearing there, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you indicate the direction from which the rocket came with a long red arrow using the marker on the diagram, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I can draw this in for you, at least the direction I thought it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Looking at the hole --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Would you give me the magic marker, please? My house was hit here (indicating) from this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From the Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This is where the Mahala begins, down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The holes from the bullets that we saw on the facade of your house, where is this facade turned to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It is turned towards the red arrow, the same side, towards the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Go on with your description, please.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I took this shot several days later. My wife and children were not there, so I took a camera and took these shots to show the state that my house was in because, of course, they were interested in seeing what had happened to the house and didn't dare go and see it for themselves. So it entered half a metre from ground level into the boiler room. On the right-hand side was where the boiler room was located, and these are the doors facing the Mahala. There is a narrow corridor between the two premises. This is the boiler room, and the rocket entered from the left-hand side, and you can see an opening in the wall half a metre up from ground level where it lodged and exploded.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That is the destruction to the ceiling of the boiler room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And this hole, what about that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That is the place of entry of the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And that hole, is it facing the direction of the Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll complete the tape there and have the lights on again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened to the son of the man who died, Sulejman Becko's son? On the evening of that day, did you have a meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Let me clarify matters. He had three sons. One son was killed in the morning. The other son was the one that I mentioned firing from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you have him in mind or the third son? Do you mean the third son?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The third son. I said that in the evening, the two of us tried to reach Zeljko Mlakic's house but that Darko had returned because he had seen a light. On the next day in the evening hours, the third son appeared, Sulejman's third son, with a woman and two children, and we asked him, "How come you're here now," and he said that he was in the basement of that particular house, the house which was half burnt down and marked in red here on the diagram. That house is built in three parts. It has a basement which is on par with the ground, on the ground level, one floor above, and a sort of basement below, below street level. And he said he was in the basement below street level in a room with a woman who was a refugee from the environs of Jajce and her children, and that they lived downstairs in the basement, below ground level. We didn't know what to do with him and them because we were afraid of all the people with weapons. And Darko thought something up quickly and, in fact, put him up, him and the woman and the children, in the house which was located behind my own house. There were two houses here, so it was sort of behind my house, Slavko Batinic's, and he was there with his wife. Slavko's house is a well-built house and protected from the front, and Darko told them to take refuge in his house because nobody could tell what was going to happen next. So he stayed on in that house for two or three days, he was put up there, and we didn't know what to say. We were very happy to see that he was alive, and we were very frightened that he wouldn't be killed ultimately, so he spent two or three days there. As we were armed with this one two-barreled rifle, Darko thought up something and said, "Well, he had an automatic rifle as a soldier. Let's ask him where his rifle is," and we went in the basement to ask him where the rifle was, and he said, "Well, I was waiting for you to ask me that," and he said that the rifle was in his own house, that is to say, the lower half of the house was not completed. There was a mound of sand, and that he had buried the rifle in this mound of sand with the ammunition. And so Darko and I, in the evening, went to recover that rifle which was buried in the sand, along with the ammunition, so that is how we came by a weapon of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened with Becko's third son in the end?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think he stayed in Slavko Batinic's house, I'm not sure how long, but six, seven, perhaps even eight days. He stayed in the house with the other people who were there, and at one point, we had to say who was located in the house because the military police arrived and they took them all away, the woman and the children and all of them. He was taken away to the part of the town that we call the colony, Kolonija. He was taken to the colony, and several days later when we got a binocular to look through, we saw him in the Mahala, so he was probably allowed to return to the Mahala at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Without describing all the shooting going on, can we take note of the fact that there was shooting on the 17th and 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. After that first day when we didn't know what was happening, there was regular gunfire. The Vitezovi shot towards the Mahala and tried to make their way towards some of the houses there and then would return. I don't know. I didn't see this, but I do know that on the right-hand side of the street, one of the Vitezovi was killed, and this left-hand side, which is where my house is situated, two of them were killed on the left-hand side, and one man was killed on the right-hand side, so that there was shooting on the 17th and 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1993, there was a strong explosion in Stari Vitez. What can you tell us about that explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You say "Stari Vitez," you're thinking of the Mahala, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I have to keep repeating that when Darko and I went up to visit our families and came back to our own house, we would stop and have something to eat and drink up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. My learned colleague has asked us to clarify something. There are two Darkos. There is Darko Kraljevic and there is your friend Darko. So when you refer to your friend Darko, would you say so?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, Darko Kraljevic was the commander of the Vitezovi, whereas Darko Mlakic was my friend who was with me all the time. He is a young man. He is about 22, 23 years old, so that is my friend, Darko. And it was with my friend Darko that I went up towards the houses where civilians were housed. We would go and have something to eat and drink. At one point in the house in which I was located, one of the men up there came into the house and told us to take refuge because there would be a loud explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Somebody, that man that came to the house. There was information from all sides, and at this particular point, a man walked in and told us not to leave the house, not to leave the premises, because there would be a strong explosion. And, yes, indeed, three to four minutes later, there was a terrible explosion which shattered the windows of the houses. In the church, all the glass fell out of the windows, and we were very frightened, and the men, I know, should have been braver, but they didn't dare go out to see what was going on for the next three or four minutes. And I, myself, saw a lot of smoke coming from the direction of my house and further on from the direction of the Mahala, so that only several days later did I actually gain information that it was a strong explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You did not see what happened. What did the people who were there tell you? What was it and who did this?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, you asked me what people had told me, the people who were there with me. In the course of our discussions, and when I talked to people, I came across practically nobody who had seen what had happened. They were just sort of popular tales and fables, one man telling another and passing the information on, and that they were sort of made up stories with regard to the amount of explosives; that explosives had been loaded into a truck and sent down there, as the road was straight, and not a long way off from the Mahala, and that they had sent a cistern down there and that was what had exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear what the idea behind this action was? What did they wish to achieve with this operation?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You did not. Very well. Thank you. Let's move onto another area. Let's try and round this section off. Could you enumerate the houses in which there were civilians, both Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Would you like me to point them out?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but please point to them a little longer and tell us the names of the owners of the houses which are on the diagram.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: So you want the position where my wife and children were and a lot of Muslims. The owner was Nikola Banic up here. That house was located up here. I cannot be certain how many people there were. It was a small house, but there might even have been 60 or 70 people located in that house. This place had persons, both Muslims and Croats. The second house where the owners of the house were Croats, and I think that all the other people there were Muslims, because it had a very strongly built basement. And the house was owned by Slavko Blaz, that was his name, the owner's name was Slavko Blaz. The third house on this side of the road, which is the same side as my own house, is Batinic Slavko's house. Slavko Batinic there was with his wife, and Sadibasic's son and the woman, I don't know her name, but she was a refugee and had come to us. And the fourth house, I know that in that house on the opposite side of the street was Ivan Tihi. And in addition to the owner and his wife, the others -- the other people put up there were Muslims, and they stayed in those houses for a considerable length of time, perhaps even as long as one month. Not in all of them, but in some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court now, please, at one point in -- during those days an incident broke out, that is to say the UNPROFOR forces arrived at the Catholic church. What happened? What was that particular event like?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I don't really know how to describe this. It wasn't really normal, but in one house there were some remaining civilians, in a house that had already caught fire. This is the house of Asim Topcic. It's this house over here. It's a three-storey house. That's the way it was. One of the brothers lived there who was not married, and the other floor was the brother who had a wife and children, and on the third floor were the parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they are Muslims. And a lady from the neighbourhood, from the house over here, happened to be there. And when the house caught fire, they were probably afraid of the shooting and they probably didn't dare go out. They picked up the phone and it so happened that the phone still worked. And one of the women from the house called the office at the church, the priest answered the phone and she said, "The house is on fire. We are burning. And we don't dare go out of the house." And then this priest went to that house and -- see how brave he was. He got them out of the house and took them into the parish house, the one where the priests live, the one next door to the church. And one woman asked them to let them use the phone so that they could make a phone call. And they did let them use the phone and she started making phone calls all over Vitez. She didn't manage to reach anyone. She reached some of her family in Zenica, though. She said that they were all alive and well and that they were at the church. That is probably the information she gave, because about half an hour later the UNPROFOR units surrounded the church very quickly, and they probably had received information that Croats were holding Muslims captive there in the church. However, the priest explained what happened, that no one was there in the church and that he was actually keeping these people in his very own apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that the kind of information that Radio Zenica had continuously been broadcasting?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that on Radio Zenica. It was really hard for me to say exactly what it was, but the Croats from Gornji Vitez turned the church into a camp and they were keeping Muslim prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now these civilians, these Muslims, lived with Croat civilians. The war is going on and days are passing by. How long did they stay there? Did anyone arrest them at any point in time, take them captive, take them prisoner? What was their treatment? How were they treated? How were Muslim civilians treated?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't tell you exactly how many days they had spent there. First of all they were not all at the same place, and in those houses they practically actually remained there until they ran short of food. And everyone brought things from their own homes. However, this went on for a considerable length of time. So then all this food that was there, that had actually been in these houses, was finished. And Nikola Banic, he had a small kiosk, a small shop across the street from his home, and that is where they had food for the longest period of time. And some of the Muslims that were in the house of Slavko Blaz, it's this house here, see, they agreed with the owner, because indeed no one came and told us anything. They didn't tell us what to do.
