And they said -- actually, one of the Muslims who was here in the house asked whether he could ask someone to give them permission to be transferred to a house that is on the same side of the street but that is closer to the church. It was one of their houses, you see, because it was over here and up there. And they all could be transferred there, so that they would be as far away from the shooting as possible. And then they indeed did move to this other house up there. So this went on for about a month or so. Some people found ways and means of reaching Travnik, Zenica. I know that some people remained there even until late in the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You are referring to 1993, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, at any point in time did anybody detain them, arrest them, lock them up, put them under guard?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no, no. I know that at these houses where they were staying they lived under the same conditions that my wife and children did. They walked all over the house. They took whatever they needed. They were not imprisoned by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any violence directed against them? Living conditions were poor for all, but was there any violence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: There was no special violence from no one's side. I know of one case, though, because there are some people who were not exactly on very good terms from the pre-war days, and I know there was one case when somebody went to seek someone else with a Muslim with whom he had quarrelled before the war, but didn't even find him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did someone move them out in the sense of putting them into trucks and leaving -- and making them leave, or did they do this individually?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They did this on their own. They realised that there was no food, that there were no clothes to wear. They sought ways and means of leaving through us. I should say, although I was in no position to help anyone, they tried to find ways and means of reaching Travnik, Zenica, so it wasn't that everyone left at the same time. But when someone would find someone over there, if there was a cease-fire or something, then one by one these families were leaving and going to Zenica or Travnik. It's not that someone herded them altogether and took them somewhere. You remember I mentioned Ahmed Topcic. He stayed. He didn't feel like going anywhere and he had no place to go. And some people tried to talk him into trying to leave too, because he had some relatives there and they had already found accommodation anywhere. Then he left and went towards Travnik. And once, after the war, I saw a picture of an exchange taking place near a bus, and I saw him and his family right by that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You described the military situation that prevailed in that part of Vitez. So tell us, please, after these first days of chaos, did you manage to get organised somehow? Did you become a soldier? Did your neighbours become soldiers? Did you get a commander? How did all of this evolve?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I described the situation to you as to how I got weapons from the mosusanta (phoen), et cetera, and then my father remembered that the man from Nova Bila, who was killed, had a weapon too. And then Darko found his weapon as well near the garden. So we had these two weapons, I don't know how to put this, military rifles. But we were so tired, because we were so frightened. We didn't dare go to sleep. Perhaps we would just doze off a bit. Then Darko Kraljevic, the commander of the Vitezovi, was going back towards the church and he was looking for these other people of ours, and he made them replace us so that we could get some rest. And day after day there were more and more of us down there. And then we asked ourselves, could we please know what is going on here and who was in charge. And we ourselves appointed Nikola Banic some kind of commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, Nikola Banic, you chose Nikola Banic to command what territory?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Perhaps it's going to seem a bit ridiculous from a military point of view, but since we had no contact with our neighbours across the road, because they were still shooting there and there were bullets flying all over and one could get killed, so we agreed that he would command this part of the street, that he would be our commander. I don't even know what to call him. And then we found out that on the other side of the street, that they had also agreed that one of them should be in charge. And then we talked about it afterwards. During those first days of the war I truly cannot remember who was in charge, Vlado Darnecar (phoen) or somebody, but at any rate, that is the way they elected one of them to take care of things and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So these were self-organised units, but when were you mobilised? When did you actually get call-up papers? When did you come to realise that you belonged to a military unit? When was this?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, there were some people who did have some knowledge of the military, and they said that this was no way to proceed. And they were shooting in the hills too. And then they knew before the war there was -- an HVO commanded the hotel or someplace like that, police wherever, and we asked these people to go there and to ask them what we were supposed to do. And I know that we succeeded in these attempts of ours. In the second half of May we received, officially, some kind of certificate saying that we belonged to some kind of unit of the Croatian Defence Council. This was my first encounter with that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And until the end of the war, is that the frontline that you remained at?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I remained at that frontline until the end of the war, that is to say where my house is, but afterwards, when there were a lot of people killed around Vitez, and when there were hardly any inhabitants left over there on those lines, and then we received some kind of orders from our commanders there that we were supposed to go to those lines too. And then they would take us there for three or four days and then we would go back, and then others would come back and then we would go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Oh, just a moment, please. So we have completed our questioning, but before we offer into evidence the three exhibits we wish to tender, could we define this map, could we show things on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that Muslim houses are depicted by little squares?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And Croat houses by triangles?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that the pink colour shows every house that was on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Red or, rather, this pink colour shows the houses that caught fire, but houses where there were only a few rooms or one room burning, those were marked differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this situation with these burned houses, how could we show this in terms of the sequence of events, dates? When did this kind of situation occur?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This situation occurred practically on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 16th of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We in our parts call it the first day of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And were there any changes afterwards, as far as the burnt houses are concerned, or did everything remain the same?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Until the war everything remained the same. And as far as the burned houses, there were others that were hit badly, but that's it as far as the houses that were on fire are concerned, because afterwards there was some kind of line, our line and Muslim line, that was established. So that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. So we would like to tender into evidence these three pieces, that is to say this map and the two other documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you permit me, there were four exhibits, because there was also a videocassette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The map which is on the easel, the two service orders, that is the call-up orders, and then the video. And the video is D516. Very well. Mr. Harmon, are you going to conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, how long about was the examination in chief? About. Flexibility.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: One hour and 55 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Two hours. Is that about how much time you are going to need, Mr. Harmon, or will it be less time than that? You don't have to take two hours, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I know, and I probably won't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. We still have another 30 minutes. I suppose you would like to begin right now. All right. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Strukar, my name is Mark Harmon. I am going to be examining you. Seated to my right is my colleague, Mr. Andrew Cayley, from the Prosecutor's office, and to his right is Mr. Gregory Kehoe. I would like to begin. I will go slow in my questions, because you need time to listen to the translation. If there is anything that's unclear, don't hesitate to ask me. Let me first of all ask a question about your background. Did you serve in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness, please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you would speak into the microphone. And when you answer my questions, if you would address the Judges, as opposed to addressing me. You can look at me when I ask the questions, but your answer should be directed towards the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And my question to you, Mr. Strukar, is when did you serve in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in what unit did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I served in the Strala S1M in light anti-aircraft units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in the course of your service in the JNA, did you receive basic infantry training?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Perhaps the answer is going to be a bit ridiculous, but I didn't really because I spent most of my time as the commander's secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But did you familiarise yourself with arms and weapons in the course of your year that you spent in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have basic courses that related to how to perform your duties as a soldier in the JNA in the event of war or with a threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. We finished that part. But I must add that it was always against some kind of imaginary enemy outside the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you left the JNA in 1976, and I take it you returned to Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That is to say all of 1976 and then the beginning of 1977, and I returned to Vitez only afterwards because you actually had to do your military service for 13 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And then, I take it from your background, you eventually went to work in the Vitezit factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were in the fire brigade, and you mentioned that you were the chief of the fire brigade, did you have any kind of training that related to physical fitness? Did you have courses? Did you have to stay fit to be a firefighter in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I belonged to the fire brigade before I went to do my service in the army, that is to say I joined up in 1973. So when I got back from the army I rejoined the fire brigade and the commander of -- I actually became the commander of this fire brigade six or seven years before this war of ours broke out. And there were no special requirements, if I understood your question correctly, in terms of physical fitness, except for the fact that firefighters, after a certain period of time, would have to take certain exams as to how to extinguish a fire, et cetera. So I went through all of that. But this was not a professional organisation. This was a voluntary fire brigade. Then these members of this brigade elected me to be their leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Vladmir Strukar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does he go by the name of Vlado?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he a neighbour of Mr. Sadibasic, the elderly gentleman you said had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to direct your attention first, Mr. Strukar, to the evening of the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We received something that may have been an inadvertent conversation taking place in the interpretation booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear my question, Mr. Strukar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The French was spared in this case. Unfortunately, but apparently it was spared. All right. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You testified on the evening of the 15th that a friend of yours came and said, and I quote, "The Muslims are preparing something." Who was that friend that came to your house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I was thinking about that, because this happened rather often, as I said, but on that key evening of the 15th it was probably Ivica Blaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was Ivica Blaz a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No. He was a driver in the fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in your neighbourhood that you have kindly drawn a diagram of, were there members of the Viteska Brigade living in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: At that time, before the war broke out, I'm thinking now, I'm trying to think of all these people, I'm trying to remember, this area (indicating) near the Catholic church, I cannot remember a single person who belonged to some of these units, so practically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know who Mario Cerkez is?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mario Cerkez. We worked in the same factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Viteska Brigade, and, if so, what role did he play?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You're trying to take me back to that time, but I simply did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am trying to take you back to that time because you've testified in great detail about that time, so I would like to ask you some questions. Did you know Mario Cerkez, and what role did he have in the Viteska Brigade? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can tell you what I know in the following sense: I heard that he was commander of that brigade, but I never had the opportunity myself of going to see him or seeing him in his capacity of commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know where his headquarters was located?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think that it was in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Turn to the Judges. I understand that it is not easy. You have the right to turn to the Prosecutor when he asks you the questions, of course, that's natural, but when you give your answers, turn to the Judges, please. Thank you very much. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The gentleman asked me whether I know where Mario had his headquarters, and my answer was that we knew that they were in the hotel and that I knew that it was in the Hotel Vitez in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the Hotel Vitez prior to the outbreak of the war, and when I'm saying "prior to the outbreak of the war," let me be more specific, within a week or two prior to the outbreak of the war in April?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: A week or two before the outbreak of the war, no, but everything that I considered to be my life, when the HVO headquarters were in the hotel, I went just once at the invitation of another man. I went up to his office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It was Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What role did Pero Skopljak have in the community?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think he was something in the civilian police, perhaps the chief of civilian police. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, on the 15th of April, 1993, in the daytime, were you at work at the Vitezit factory or were you at home or were you somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Quite certainly on the few days prior to the 15th, I was waiting. I was on this waiting list at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you were probably at home on the 15th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, in your community, did you see any unusual activity taking place with HVO soldiers moving about, anything different and out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No. If you listened to me when I was talking, I said that there were night watches, together, separate, or so on, but on those days, there was no night watch set up, nor was anything taking place at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So on the 15th of April, 1993, you don't recall anything unusual taking place in your community in respect of the movement of HVO soldiers or the presence of HVO soldiers; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Then I understood your testimony to be that after your friend, perhaps Ivica Blaz, came to your house and said, "The Muslims are preparing something," and that was around 7.30 in the evening, that you and others gathered, 15 to 20 neighbours gathered near or in the square near the church. Were the 15 to 20 people who gathered in the square near the church all Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with any of those 15 to 20 neighbours to find out what it was that was about to happen?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, naturally we talked, because, as I said, this was not the first time. These kinds of alarms occurred previously, and it was just so much smoke without fire. So these people and Ivica Blaz, who told me on that particular evening that something was wrong, was one of those people who were prone to create a little more panic than was absolutely necessary, at least that's what we thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand. But what was it that you were told was going to happen, if you were told anything at all?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, word for word, he told me that it would be a good idea for me to go up there because it appeared that the Muslims were preparing something, words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you say, "What is that something they were preparing?" Did you ask him what it was, to be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, because it had happened on several occasions before that, and when I testified, I said that we had problems with the cistern and other things in the course of the day, I don't want to tire you with that, some shooting. Someone would come with a car, he would be stopped, and then there would be shooting on the street. There were sort of alarms of this kind. We considered it to be the normal run of things at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, given that you were on a heightened state of alert yourself because something might happen, did you see anything unusual in your community in respect of the Muslims who lived in your community?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you didn't see any Muslim armed people walking around in your community the night before the attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct or that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see any armed Muslims walking in your community the night of the 15th of April or the early morning of the 16th of April prior to the commencement of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as I understand your testimony, you went home, but at 11.30 to midnight, your friend, again, returned and said, "Get out. Something is amiss." And you went back to the square, and, again, as I understood your testimony, there were a large number of people in the square. Did I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, you understood it correctly, but you just said "many people," and a moment ago, you said "15 to 20 people," so those were the same people who were there at around 7.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So at 11.30, were the same people who had been in the square at 7.30 still in the square at 11.30 to 12.00?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, because I said that we had agreed that half of us would go home, and that after midnight, they would wake us up when they had had enough and send us there. And that was the time from the beginning of the war conflicts in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was quite normal that somebody would be awake all night and patrol the house, around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were there any Muslims in the square when you returned the second time, that is, around 11.30 or midnight?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you, on that second occasion, ask your friend, "What was it that was amiss?" Did you get any additional details?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, quite naturally, I was interested in knowing, but the information was coming in very sparsely. It was difficult to arrive at any information. People were just saying that there is something wrong, we don't know what it is, but there was nothing concrete, nothing said in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you, based on your personal observations, see anything that looked to you to be amiss?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Not at that point, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after you returned to the square the second time, as I understand your testimony, and please correct me because my notes are a little bit unclear here, you went back to your house to get your family and went to your parents' house to get your parents out of their house, and you tried to get additional information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: More or less, yes, that is correct, what you noted, but I said that first I took my wife and my children, and then they told me up there, "Where are your father and mother? It would be a good idea if they were safe," and I said that this had already happened on previous occasions. We were afraid for the lives of our wives and children and parents, that they would be the first to be attacked, but at least five or six times, don't hold me to that figure, in the course of the summer of 1992 up to those events, they would be taken up there to sleep and be brought back and start the whole process over again. So it did not seem to be anything unusual for that particular occasion, out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, during this time period that we've just talked about, somebody told you you should not worry because the men from Nova Bila had arrived?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I was not told this directly, I don't think I said that, but as our wives and children and the females who were in the house, there was not enough room for all of us in the house, so we were outside the house, and people would be coming all the time, and there were some funny incidents. Somebody would fall down the stairs. I don't remember who said what, but information had arrived, not only to me, they told all of us, "You needn't worry. Some young men have come from the direction of Nova Bila," and they said that we shouldn't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you understand that those young men who had come from Nova Bila to be HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: At that time, that's what I thought, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what time did you receive that information, that you did not have to worry, that men from Nova Bila had arrived? Do you recall, approximately, what time that was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It is difficult to say now, to give you the exact minute and hour, but it was in the morning around 4.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you had gone back to a particular house with your family, had you not, and you took refuge in a particular house with your family after you retrieved them; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You said that I had taken them to safety, and I thought, as a man, I needn't take cover, take safety in the house, so we were all around the house where our women and children were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you remained outside with your friends?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, there were two houses and some outhouses, so there was enough space to move around outside all these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you kindly take the pointer that's in front of you and just point on the diagram that you prepared, where was the house where your family had taken refuge?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: There are two houses there (indicating) belonging to Mr. Nikola Banic. In front is an old house, and this is the new house with a stronger-built basement. So you enter the old house from this side, and from the other side, the new house. So they were in the old house and in the new house, and we were moving around outside, around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it's a house that is located not far from the Catholic church in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you testified next that you, at some point in time, heard a strong explosion. Do you remember approximately what time it was that you heard that explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It is difficult to say exactly what the time was, but I do remember that it was dawn, and as it was mid-April, it could have been somewhere around 6.00 a.m., because I know that it was dawn but not light enough to be daylight, so it was still dusk. So I don't know what time day breaks at that time of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were you specifically when you heard that explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I was situated here (indicating) by these houses where the families were. There is a house here belonging to Mirko Blaz, and there are some sheds here, wood sheds, and so on, so there was a little shelter there, and I was here (indicating), next to Mirko Blaz's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you inside a shelter?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, up to the point in time where you heard that explosion at dusk, had you seen any Muslims with arms walking in and around or through your community?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you notice any unusual activity in and around the Muslim houses prior to hearing that large explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, once you heard the loud explosion, to your knowledge, if you know that, was it a shell that detonated? Was it a cannon or a large weapon firing? Can you describe what you heard?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, in addition to what you asked me about my military experience, that is to say, from my past, at that time, I didn't know any of this. It was an explosion, a little stronger than the ones I had heard before that when some grenades exploded, because at that time, some people had grenades of this kind and would throw them at shop windows, but this time, it was a somewhat stronger explosion, and in the course of the war later on, I realised that it was a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you reconstructed from the noise later on to conclude that the noise you had heard initially was a mortar; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know where the mortar came from, the firing came from? Were you able to reconstruct that as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no, because at that moment, at that time, where we were located, nobody, and especially me and all of us there, we could not have known. Perhaps we had heard this earlier on, had we been accustomed to hearing a noise of this kind, but it was just a strong explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So as you sit here today, can you testify whether that mortar was fired by the HVO or by the Muslims or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's 1.00. Mr. Strukar, thank you, we will continue at some point after lunch. I have no further questions at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to try to organise our work. We said that we would have our Status Conference at 2.30, but it might be more appropriate to finish with Mr. Strukar. About how much more time do you need, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think we're proceeding at a decent rate, Mr. President, perhaps another hour, but I don't want to be held to that. I certainly will complete my examination within the hour and fifty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. If Judge Shahabuddeen agrees, I think that we would release the witness this afternoon, which means that we would start at 2.30 with Mr. Strukar, and then after about an hour and a half, which would correspond with the afternoon break, before we move to hear the next witness, we would have our closed session Status Conference. Do you agree with that, Mr. Hayman? All right. Mr. Strukar, you'll be here again at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the witness brought in, please, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, we are going to continue with the cross-examination. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, we will continue with the cross-examination now. I wanted to go out of the sequence that we were following in your testimony just to revisit an issue, and that is on either the 14th of April, 1993 or the 15th of April, 1993 did you go to the fire station where you were the chief of the volunteer fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think that I did. I think I did, yes, because they were sort of regular visits to the fire station to see what was new there, and I would return after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you testified that the Muslim Territorial Defence forces were located either in the same building or next door to the building of the fire brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see any unusual activity at the fire -- at the Territorial Defence offices on either the 14th or the 15th of April, activity that was out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, I did not see that, because I only moved along the street from my home to the fire station, which is also along the same street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Strukar, I would like to return to where we left off on the cross-examination just before lunch. That point was that we were discussing the explosion that you heard around dusk, and I believe your testimony was, on direct examination, that after you heard that explosion that you heard some shooting from nearby. Would that be small arms fire, rifle fire that you were describing?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It was the explosion in the morning hours that I spoke about. If you are talking about that, I did not say there was shooting from close-up, but from that direction. I heard a burst of gunfire, small arms gunfire, from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say "that direction," which direction are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The direction from this house where I was at the time on the left-hand side of the Lasva River, from the direction of the Lasva River, which means from that side. And at the time I was not able to assess the distance, how far away it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you able to assess who was shooting, whether it was the HVO or whether it was some other party?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: My assessment is -- of course I could not give any exact assessment. What we could see beside the houses went up to the Lasva River. Across from the river there are several houses inhabited by Croats and we knew that from the distance that these houses were that this was further up, where there were no more houses, just a petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your direct examination you then said that you went to a particular location and you saw Muslim civilians starting to arrive, and that those Muslim civilians had said to you that the men from Bila had expelled them from their own houses. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I remember that part of my testimony, but what you have just said, that this was the men from Bila, I said that. I did say that. But, in fact, they did not know who it was, who had done this. I don't know if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Everybody was crying general -- everybody saying something. So it was difficult to discern what they were saying and whether that was actually what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, let me focus on that particular series of events in your testimony. What time of the morning was it that you first saw these Muslim civilians arriving to your location?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, shall we say that a point for measuring time was from the explosion that I heard, which means that it was 10, 15 minutes after the explosion had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, approximately -- when these Muslims arrived, are you referring to men, women and children? Can you describe the Muslims, how many there were, and the composition of the group that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think -- I saw this group where my family was. That's the group I saw most often. And there were men there and women and children of all ages. And also that is parts of our family, my own family and the families of others, so that there were, as I said, some 60 to 70 civilians located in that particular house. And of that number, I can't tell you exactly, but, say, half, half. Half were Croats, half were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were any of the Muslims that you saw fleeing toward your direction armed with any type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no. But people said that the young men who stormed their houses had been looking for arms and said "surrender your arms."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the group of Muslims we've been discussing, did they appear to you to be frightened?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: We all were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- did you have a chance, you personally have a chance, to talk to some of these Muslims who had sought refuge at a house where you were?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I talked to them, but I can't tell you exactly whether this was straightaway in the morning or in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, will you tell the Judges what those Muslims told you that happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They were ordinary reactions, that is when I saw that they could talk to somebody of the Croat ethnic group and that they could get information from me, they would usually say, "Well, what's all this? What's going on? What's all this happening?" But -- and those were the type of questions that they asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they tell you that members of the HVO had attacked their houses, had entered their houses?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Not formulated in that particular way. I cannot assert that they formulated it in that way, but we understood something of the kind. They did not explain anything much. They just asked us what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To the best of your ability, do you recall, Mr. Strukar, can you tell the Judges how they formulated what had happened to them that morning?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Let me tell you in the following way. Perhaps you are generalising matters, that they had all come at the same time, whereas they would come family by family from one house and another house. It wasn't a sort of general stand. And when we asked what had happened, they said that they had knocked on their doors, asked for arms, and sent us towards this house. Nobody brought them to the house. They just said, "Go up there where all the others are."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say the Muslims said "they," who did you understand "they" to mean?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I thought that these people, the people who were there in the houses, because the times were such that you didn't ask a lot of questions, especially if you were afraid. Quite simply, it was better for you not to ask if you see something on fire. You know that lots of things could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. Strukar, you understood my question. In response to my question, two questions ago, you answered, "And when we asked what had happened, they said that they had knocked on their doors." And my question was: Who were the Muslims referring to when they said, "They knocked on our doors?"

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Quite obviously, they had in mind the people who were there. You see, it was an event. Their houses were on fire, they were shooting, and they were conscious of the fact that it wasn't me, that it wasn't the people who were there, but the people over there, not those of us who were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let me change the topic briefly. If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 105, please, shown to the witness. Mr. Strukar, while the Registrar is getting Prosecutor's Exhibit 105 to show you, you testified that at some point in time that morning of the 16th of April that you saw an anti-aircraft gun on the back of a truck arrive in your area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, I saw it in the late morning hours parked near my father's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 105. Mr. Usher, it needs to be changed. It's the wrong -- and perhaps I will show it first on this computer screen. But then if you could take that exhibit and show it to the witness, because it's a small image. Hand it to the witness. Let me ask you, Mr. Strukar, is this the anti-aircraft gun on the back of a truck that you saw on the morning of the 16th of April 1993? Does it appear to be similar to it?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's it. Because it looked something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Strukar. Now, that anti-aircraft gun was in the possession of the HVO, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You keep referring to the HVO, but at the time it belonged to those young men who had come on that particular morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, those were members of an armed force group, were they not? They were members of the -- let me backtrack. Were those men wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I said that -- I saw some of them in the course of the day later on, and, yes, some of them were wearing vests, camouflage sorts of vests, and green jumpers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they have HVO patches on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty because they are insignia which could not have been seen. You couldn't see what somebody had on his arm, but I know that around their arms, they had white bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which side of the conflict did you think they represented, the Croat side or the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I thought they represented the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you, in respect of the white bands that you've described, could you give me a little bit better picture of what those white bands looked like, where they were? Were they attached to the uniform? Were they hanging from the uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I'll try. Perhaps I'll discover this tomorrow or the day after, but they were individual for each soldier, depending on how they had placed this, and the day after or the day after that, I got a band like that, and I pinned it on so that it was hanging downwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did the white band that you received signify?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It signified a sort of permit to be able to move around, not to be shot at and killed by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers with white ribbons hanging from their uniforms on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: On the 16th, that is the first day, yes, I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, do you know the significance of those white ribbons that were hanging from those soldiers' shoulders?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: At the time, I did not; however, after the war, those ribbons changed. Sometimes they were red, sometimes white, and at other times blue, depending on who would determine what coloured bands were to be worn one day and the other, so that the enemy would have a different coloured ribbon and so that there would be nothing mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So those white bands and, later on what you learned, other coloured ribbons were bands that were on the soldiers' shoulders in order to identify them as, for example, Croat soldiers and not Muslim soldiers; is that right? It was a matter of identification.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it was, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when was the first time that you were in the Lasva Valley, Mr. Strukar, that you ever saw white ribbons hanging from soldiers' shoulders. Was it the morning of the 16th of April, 1993 or had you seen that type of ribbon hanging from a soldier's shoulder prior to the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, I had not seen them previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that, in other parts of Vitez and in other villages in the Lasva Valley, including Ahmici, the Croat soldiers were wearing similar types of ribbons hanging from their shoulders on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no, because what we saw on the first two or three days, that was in a very small region and not very far from where my family was located and the house where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Later on in the morning of the 16th of April, as I understood your testimony, additional Muslims came running from the area of the Catholic church, in that general vicinity, and you testified on direct examination that they were crying, that you could see flames from houses in that particular area, and that they, the Muslims, had said that their houses had been set on fire. Do you remember that portion of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was what it was, more or less, but it was a group of Muslim civilians who came to the house where my own family was, my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, who did they say had set their houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: There were no names mentioned. Quite simply, they were conscious of the fact that it wasn't us and that we were the ones who should help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they say that other Croats had set their houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: More or less, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did they say that those other Croats were armed with weapons at the time they set their houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they said that they had weapons, and they asked us who they were because they didn't know them either, and we didn't know them because they were not our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you conclude that the people who set the Muslims' houses on fire may have been the soldiers from Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: We would find out about that only a few days later as things developed further, when we realised what was going on, when we managed to talk, and then we asked each other whether anyone had recognised these people, and that is how we found out that they had come from Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you then, later in the morning, I take it, you went then to try to find your father at his house. Approximately what time of the day was that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I said that it was late in the morning, perhaps 10.00 or 10.30, up to 11.00 a.m. at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I can just have a minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you arrived at your father's house later that morning, your father, was he the next door neighbour of Mr. Sulejman Sadibasic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Sadibasic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your father have a weapon in his house, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: My father did not have any military weapons, but I know, when I was a child, that he had some kind of a pistol because he worked at the electric public utilities company, but I hadn't seen that particular pistol for a long, long time, so I don't know whether he did have any weapons then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the assistance of the registrar? Could I see Prosecutor's Exhibit 102, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, I'm going to show you some photographs and I'm going to ask you to identify them. Let me show you the three photographs I'd like to show you first, and then we will place them on the ELMO, which is the machine to your left, so that the public can see these as well, but let me show these to you first so you can take a look at them, and the image, I think, is much better when you take a look at them before they're placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It would be better not to put these photographs on the ELMO because they were admitted as confidential documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have a set for the Judges? Well, I'm not sure how the Judges are supposed to check on the work that is being done in the courtroom if -- at least one so that Judge Shahabuddeen and I could verify what the document is saying about the photographs that are being shown to him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Once they've been chosen, we can first show them to you, and then show them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There are no other copies, is what you're saying. All right, Mr. Hayman is going to do us a service. I want to thank you very much, Mr. Hayman. I can promise you that, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, thank you for bringing that to our attention. We will not show these on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could show these to the witness, and we'll start with the photograph, Mr. Strukar, that is marked 232.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Actually, if you would take a look at 232, 233, and 234, the three photographs, first of all, take a look at those photographs, the three of them, do you recognise the body to be that of Mr. Sulejman Sadibasic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is the body of Sulejman Sadibasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And he is in front of a house that appears to be burned. Was that his house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as you look up the road in the direction that the gun barrel is pointed, on the left-hand side next to Mr. Sadibasic's house, there's a house that is not burned. Whose house is that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You said next to Sadibasic's house?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. In this ...

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That is Zeljko Mlakic's house. When I testified, I told you about him. He was ill and he was at home with his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right. Is Zeljko Mlakic a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And proceeding next to Zeljko Mlakic's house, there appears to be another house. Whose house is that; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think it is registered in the name of Marijan Mlakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Mlakic is also a Croat, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I think photograph 233 is just, you'll see, a slightly different image, a different perspective, of this very same image that's shown in 232, and the same is true in 234, it's a closer image. So let me ask you some questions then about your visit to your father's house and your viewing of the body of Mr. Sulejman Sadibasic. There has been testimony in this case from the person who took this photograph that it appeared that Mr. Sadibasic had had his throat cut. Did you go close to Mr. Sadibasic's body and did you inspect it?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no, I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see what appeared to be bullet wounds of any kind in the body of Mr. Sadibasic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that either because I never approached the dead body. There's a distance involved from there to my father's house, it's about 30 metres away, and I saw him from that distance, and not even from this angle, but from the left-hand side through the garden. That's the way I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you saw the body of Mr. Sadibasic, did you see any weapons near his body?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, you said in your testimony as well that some time later -- and I'm finished with those photographs, you can give them back to the usher, if you want -- some time later, I believe you said you saw some other bodies in and around the house of Mr. Sadibasic, and I wasn't sure when it was that you saw those other bodies. Was it on the 16th or was it a few days later?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, it wasn't on the 16th. It was considerably later because even the unfortunate Sadibasic remained lying there by the road for a long time, I can't remember exactly how long, but about seven or eight days, and rumours -- people were wondering where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How old was Mr. Sadibasic, the one whose image is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I never really thought about it, and now I'm trying to think in relation to my own father. Well, I don't know, probably around 60. I really don't know. He even looked a bit older than his age.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, please assist me if you can, approximately how many days later was it that you saw the bodies of Sulejman's son and two other bodies that you marked on the diagram that you prepared? How many days after the 16th of April was it that you saw those bodies?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You're trying to get a very precise answer from me, but I can't really give you that kind of answer, six or seven or eight or ten days, I don't know, but I could not see them from the part where we were. So my friend Darko and I, we were planning this, how we could get closer to Sulejman's body so that we could bury it, but, I don't know, I think it was about ten days or so. The Croats who were there from the upper side, they tried to stop these UNPROFOR tanks to ask them to put them away. I can't tell you exactly, seven or eight days, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, that's fair, it's been many years ago, and I'm not trying to pin you down to a particular date, I'm just trying to get an approximation. But when you ultimately returned and saw these other three bodies, the son of Sulejman and the other two bodies, did you go close to those bodies and did you inspect them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you get close enough to see how they had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no, no, because after these seven, eight, or ten days or whatever, no, no, it wasn't really acceptable at all for me to get that close.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you told us or you told my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, about information that you had heard from a third party about how Mr. Sadibasic had been killed. I believe you said he had been a Serb. Did you ever have an opportunity, Mr. Strukar, to talk to the wife of Mr. Sadibasic and inquire of Mrs. Sadibasic how her husband was killed and how her sons were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no, not until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you know Mrs. Sadibasic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is she an honest woman?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you in respect of who --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sorry, you really confused me a bit there, but in their family, the older members of the family, Sulejman and his son, those who were killed, they really had a fine reputation among us, the neighbours, whereas his wife and another son did not. That is why I said "no" in response to your question, that that was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mrs. Sadibasic has a different assessment of how her family was killed than your Serb -- your friend with whom you had a discussion. What she says happened is that on the morning of the 16th, soldiers came to her house, they knocked on their windows, they were shouting, "Balijas, Vitez is ours." They had white bands around their arms, that their uniforms were black, that they took her two sons, Safet and Sifet, outside, they were alive. In addition, they had broken into her house and took the sons out. They struck her in the back of her head with a rifle butt, she identifies the people who did that, and then she was forced outside. She says that when she went outside, she saw her two sons were alive and in the custody of the soldiers who had taken them outside, that the soldiers who were guarding them had camouflage uniforms on and that they had started to take away her two sons. She then fled, and she identifies a number of Muslim houses that she saw were on fire. Now, is it, in your opinion, equally likely or more likely that Mrs. Sadibasic knows more about what happened to her husband and to her sons than the neighbour you have given hearsay information about or do you have an opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Possibly quite a few things happened because it's her house, after all, but it's not really clear to me. You asked a few minutes ago how old my neighbour was. If they were shooting elderly people, how come she stayed alive? I mean, it's not really clear to me. How could she escape?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not here to answer questions. The Judges can draw whatever conclusions they want from how she happened to survive and how it was that her husband and her son were murdered, so the Judges will draw the inferences and any conclusions they want from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Move to another question, please. There were suggestions, hypotheses being bandied about what was, might have been, and this or that circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to a different subject, and that is that on a date sometime after the 16th of April you returned to your house and you showed us and commented on a video film that I believe you took showing the remnants of a rocket of some kind. And you identified, I think, you identified that rocket and the remains of that rocket to have come from a multi-rocket launcher. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That's the way it is, approximately. However, I have to explain to the Judges that afterwards, during the course of the war, I saw that this was a rocket that is used in a multiple rocket launcher and that both sides on the war did this. They would take out one barrel. They would only use one barrel, really. I don't know how many grenades there are there. And that is why I am talking about one barrel of a multiple rocket launcher, not a multiple rocket launcher as such. However, what I had filmed, I filmed a few days after the house had been hit. I was trying to explain to my wife and family what the house looked like, because we had moved into the house only a few months before that, so I got this little camera and I tried to film for them what had happened to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to please pull Prosecutor's Exhibit 82, please. Now, if these photographs could be put on the ELMO one at a time starting with Z2/461, which is the first photograph in there. Mr. Strukar, I am going to ask you just a number of questions. Can you see those images clearly on the ELMO before you on the computer screen before you? Do you recognise that image of that particular weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I can see this image clearly. I can see it's some kind of a gun, but I never saw this in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These images, for your information, are photographs that were taken by the members of the British battalion, and these are HVO weapons that they have testified about and have testified were present in the Lasva Valley. Did you ever see the image, this particular weapon in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the next image, Mr. Usher. Have you ever seen this particular weapon before?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It's not the same thing, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't believe it is. It is? Well, I stand -- we will get some testimony on it. It may be. If it is -- We'll turn to the next image, which is Z2/463. Have you ever seen that kind of a weapon in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: May I see the photograph itself, please, because I cannot see it at all here. No, I don't really. I don't know what this is either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, we are going to turn to 465, Z2/465. This is a multi-rocket launcher. Did you ever see a weapon similar to this in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You keep asking me whether I saw things in the Lasva River Valley, and I said this concerns the Lasva River Valley that I spent most of the war by my own home. I went out to the outer lines a few times, but I was an infantryman in the trenches. I didn't really see this kind of thing, but I did see it after the war, but I didn't know who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Can we turn to this image, please, the next image, 468. Do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that kind of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I saw it only in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn to Z2/469. Do you recognise the man who is holding the large rifle in his left hand in that image?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to miss. I would like to know exactly who this is. I know the man in the blue sweatshirt, but I'm not sure about the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who is the man in the blue sweatshirt?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Jako Krizanac is his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's the man on the left-hand side of this particular image?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. A dark blue sweatshirt with a red collar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Usher. I am finished with that exhibit. Mr. Strukar, the rocket shell that you recovered or observed in your house, did it have any kind of markings that would attribute it to one side of the conflict, the Muslim side, or the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you see that rocket being launched toward your house, or did you just see the smoke -- hear the detonation and see the smoke coming from your house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The latter. At the moment when the explosion was heard, I looked in the direction of my house and I saw smoke. I did not see when the rocket shell actually came.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time the rocket shell exploded on your house, was there fighting of some kind going on in and around Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You mean the very moment when the explosion occurred? I told you about some of our wartime experiences. We thought that morning that war was when you could hear a lot of shooting only, but afterwards we realised that only if you hear a few bullets that that's war too. But at that point I cannot really recall how intensive the shooting was. However, there was shooting. There were also rifle grenades and other explosions, because -- I would like to tell you also that the houses were on fire and sometimes something would explode, for example, in somebody's attic, and you would think that somebody had been shooting before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn briefly to some very short items that you covered in your direct examination. One of the items you testified about was that a young man by the name of Samet Sadibasic, son of the deceased man we saw a moment ago, was taken, and then you said a few were captured on the morning of the 16th of April. Then you testified that sometime later you saw him in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I did not say that he was captured on the 16th. I just said that he spent a day or two in the basement of his house with another woman, not with his own wife, because he is not married, and also children. And when he felt that the situation was a bit more quiet, he went out on his own and he walked up to us. And then he stayed at Slavko Batinic's house for a while, six or seven, eight days, I really don't know for how long, and then the police took him away somewhere in the direction of the town. But afterwards we saw him running from one side to the other from the Mahala side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do you know that the police took him to the cinema where he was detained for a considerable period of time, and where he was then forced to dig trenches for the HVO? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no. Because the first contacts -- actually, I didn't even see him. But a friend of mine asked him what happened to him, and I said the military police took him away. And he said, "I've just seen him in the Mahala." So then we could see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to your testimony about the large bomb, large detonation that went off. We've referred to it in this courtroom as the truck bomb explosion. You said in your testimony that a man came to your house shortly before the large explosion that you heard detonated, informed you there would be a large explosion. Who was that man who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I didn't say he came to my house, but he came up there where we were all moving around and where I was when I went to visit my family. And who said it exactly, I really can't say, but someone just shouted that we should take refuge and nobody should go outside. And this lasted one, two, three days, so people were getting a little restless going around the house. They would go out to light a cigarette and so on. He said that nobody should move around and quite simply we huddled down there by the houses and waited to see what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question was who was it who warned you about the bomb?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I can't remember, because, as I say, we weren't just sitting there and somebody came up to us to tell us something. It was just somebody shouting. For example, I would like to say something that isn't appropriate for this Court. And they would just say, "Get the hell out of there. Get inside. Get inside." So that they thought that something might be happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you find out after the explosion had occurred that others in your community, other Croats in your community had been warned in advance, like you had been warned, that there was going to be an explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss it, because as I said before, it was better to keep quiet on some matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Because from the 16th onwards everything that we had seen up until then, on television and what was going on in the Republic of Croatia, in Sarajevo, in Gorazde or whatever, we quite simply saw that people were being killed and that it was very possible to lose one's life, and what people were capable of doing. So we tried to save our lives and ask as little questions as possible, regardless of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After the explosion, did you inquire about who was responsible for the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Wasn't that the biggest explosion that took place in the whole war, in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think it was, at least from what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But you didn't inquire as to who was responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I don't think you seem to realise, to understand me and the others who did not feel ourselves to be soldiers, and so quite simply the less questions we asked, the better for us. You asked what happened after -- that was during the war. You asked what happened afterwards. Well, in Mahala several Croat houses -- several Croatian houses, and when they went up towards us, they told us that it was a cistern. All we knew was that there was a truck. And they told us then that they had been told that it was a cistern containing explosives. And so we arrived at some information to fill in the puzzle. We got bits and pieces to our puzzle to complete the puzzle. But we kept that information to ourselves and kept ourselves to ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One last question on the subject matter, Mr. Strukar. Since you lived relatively close to the site of this detonation, at any time after the detonation occurred did any member of the HVO military police or the HVO army or the police in any capacity come to you or come to others in the neighbourhood and ask what, if anything, you knew about the detonation of that large truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to another area of your examination, and that is that you testified that after the 16th of April a number of Muslims remained in your small community in and around, let's say, the Catholic church area. Approximately how many Muslims was that that remained in and around your particular area, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You've asked me this for the second or third time, that is to say you are asking me figures. I never counted. I haven't done so until the present day. But it was from my house towards the church, everybody who was there then, all the Muslims, the men, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then you testified, and I had a sense that you had more of an appreciation for numbers, because you testified in your direct examination that for about a month some of the Muslims remained until summertime and -- so I had a sense that you had a feeling about how many Muslims there were that were in your community. You testified some left, you testified some remained --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, but those were names, because up until the summer, those who remained until the summer, there were four or five of them, and you couldn't state their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So up until the summer or in the summertime there were about four or five Muslims who remained in your particular area. Did I understand your testimony right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Those who had left, but some of them had stayed on after that and are there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Had the vast majority of the Muslims who lived in your portion of the community left Vitez by the summertime?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And after the summertime of 1993 did more of those Muslims leave until only a small number -- actually, did only a small number of Muslims then remain throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I'm afraid I might not have understood the question, but as you say -- did you say that after the war people -- after the summer the people continued to leave, the summer of 1993, whether any of them left? Is that what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, the last one left, Topcic, with his wife and children, and then nobody left after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were the Muslims who remained in your community fearful, were they afraid of the HVO? Were they afraid of the Croats, were they afraid of the military police, and were they afraid of the Special Purposes Units, such as the Vitezovi and the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. We were all afraid, and I am purposely saying all of us in the sense of myself and my family and them, because we didn't know what could happen, as there was shooting on all sides, in all parts of Vitez, and we knew that people did die. So we were all afraid, and they were too. And they wanted to ask what they should do. So they were afraid, if that is the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to separate, if I can for a moment, general fear of something that might happen to them because a war is going on from a specific fear that the remaining Muslims had vis-a-vis the HVO, vis-a-vis Croats. Were the Muslims who remained -- and you had contact with them -- did they express a fear, the type of which I have just described?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Let me answer in the following way. After that they were not afraid of us Croats who were there, their neighbours, but they were always afraid that somebody might come in from outside, from elsewhere, who did not know them. Because they saw situations in which when some Croats did not want to come down to my house to set up a sort of defence line, that the Vitezovi, for example, would compel the Croats to do so, threatening them with weapons and firing the weapons above their heads.
