So they saw that you couldn't joke around with people like that, but you had to do what they wanted you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the last area of inquiry that I have, Mr. Strukar, is you have prepared this diagram to your left, and I believe the houses with triangles are Croat houses, is that right, on your diagram?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it appears that the houses, some Croat houses were burned on the 16th of April, 1993, and those appear to be indicated with red; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But I said that this diagram was composed on the basis of my recollections and the first two or three days when there were things going on. And on the first, second and third day I can say with full responsibility here today that it all appeared to be just one day. It all merged into one day. So I can't tell you what actually happened on the first, second, third or fourth day. It all merged into one day for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand. The question I am going to ask you, though, is did you see any of those Croat houses intentionally set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The house belonging to Vojislav Mlakic was on fire on, let's say, the first day, and quickly after that the fire was extinguished, the next day or the day after, but don't hold me to that. I don't know exactly what day it was. And looking at it from my house, from the vantage point of my house, I saw some young men from the lower side throwing something at the house, and the house was then set alight. When I say "something," perhaps it was some liquid. So then it was set alight, it burnt, and then from this lower side I saw somebody throwing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you identify those men?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know if those men were Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I cannot say, but I thought they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And would you point out on that diagram which house you are referring to. For the record, Mr. Registrar, what Exhibit number is that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's 513, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness is pointing, for the record, to the lower right-hand triangulated house coloured in red. The lowest house on the right-hand side of Defence Exhibit 513. Thank you very much, Mr. Strukar, for pointing that out to us. Mr. Strukar, let me ask you then one additional question. In respect of the Muslim houses that were burned in your community, did you see any of those houses being set on fire, or do you know the circumstances under which they caught fire?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, I really cannot say. I really don't know that. From the place where I was, I did not see that. I just saw them burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And after these events of the 16th and the early phase of the war, you said you eventually became a member of the HVO, and you became, I thought I heard you say, an infantry soldier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you were in the Viteska brigade, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You mean the commander of the Vitez brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The first in line you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As I've already said, we first elected a commander from amongst ourselves, and that was Nikola Banic, and then later on it emerged that somebody commanded all the houses that I spoke about. And after that there was Vlado Drmic. However, later on again, in the second half of May, nothing was going right, so in the middle of the summer a new command was established with a new commanding officer, and it was Marko Blaz. Marko Blaz, I'm sorry, Marko Blaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, thank you very much. You have been very patient. I appreciate it. Mr. President, I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nobilo? So the exhibits which were filed were which exhibits, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The exhibits that I used were old exhibits which had previously been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, I am going to try very briefly to go ahead now. Starting with Sadibasic's house, which was half burnt. Can you name the Croat owners of the houses which were burnt on or around the 16th of April, 1993, on your part of the street, on your side of the road?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You mean these houses towards Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, between Sadibasic and the Mahala, which houses were burnt on the 16th of April, '93.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This here is the house belonging to Marijan Mlakic, which was burnt from this side, and then the fire was extinguished. This is a dual building, a little larger, a larger building, owned by Nikola Mlakic and Zorka Mlakic. On the diagram I drew in two buildings. They had several of them, perhaps three or four. Some of them belonged to Nikola and some to Zorka, to the owner of this house, and that is Vojislav Mlakic's house here. So those were the Croat houses which were burnt, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you enumerate the Croat owners on the opposite side of the street towards the Mahala, opposite to your side of the road, which was partially burnt or completely burnt.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The first in line is Zvonko Mlakic's house, then behind his house there are a series of buildings, such as the summer house and the shed, and I know that the fire was put out afterwards. And this house -- and Nikola Krizanac's shop. Those were the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you were all afraid and that the Muslims were afraid, the ones that remained, that stayed behind. According to your overall knowledge, when did the incidents take place, either towards the Muslims or even -- the Muslim houses, that is to say, set alight, so not only in your neighbourhood, as far as you knew, when did these incidents occur?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As far as the burning of their houses is concerned, I can refer to them as one incident, a single incident, because practically all the Muslim houses were set fire to on that particular morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the Vitez municipality as a whole. In the course of 1993 when a house was set alight, how did this happen? What was the general view?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you the general view. I can only tell you my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, give us your opinion then.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, it is my opinion that these were usually people who looted the houses and then set fire to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us return to the evening of the 15th. Did you, at any given moment, go to reconnoitre or have a look at what was happening in the Mahala and whether the Muslims in the Mahala were preparing for any kind of conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no, I never even thought of doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, we can conclude that you do not know whether the Muslims were preparing in the Mahala or not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is what can be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Those from Nova Bila, how many of them came? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I really cannot. I really can't because all I saw was three or four of them running around. I really don't know how many there were, even approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you think was the purpose of the soldiers from Nova Bila sending Muslim civilians in the direction of the houses where Croatian civilians were already located? Why did they do this? What was your opinion? What did you conclude then or later on?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, this was never quite clear to me, except, quite simply, that they wanted to get them away from the area in which they were. You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where were they? Were they up at the frontline?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, these people from Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They moved towards the line where this line would be established, so all the Muslims from those houses, they were sent up together with the other Croatian civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The vast majority of Croatian civilians, had they already left, evacuated, their Croatian houses in the same area?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Vitez around the church, you knew Sadibasic and that he was a good man, and other people knew him as well, most probably. Tell me whether you ever heard that anybody slaughtered him, slit his throat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, I heard that for the first time in this courtroom here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us quite frankly and honestly, we are in a court of law, Sadibasic's wife, was she capable of lying in a situation of this kind? What do you think? What's your opinion knowing her?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As I said to the Prosecutor a moment ago, I don't like talking about her, but I really do not have a good opinion of her, because we neighbours up there, neighbours of hers, thought that, in fact, she had spoiled her sons, her two sons, and that they stole and so on, whereas their father and the ones who had died were really good people, honest people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you do not feel that Sadibasic's wife was an honourable woman, an honest woman, and a woman of high moral qualities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, if we're going to get into the considerations about the honesty of somebody else who -- well, let's go through that very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Prosecutor was quoting what that woman had said, and I thought that it was important for us to know something about this woman, but I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I just made a comment. I could have made the same comment to the Prosecutor. Let us never forget that we are here in the trial of General Blaskic for extremely serious crimes, and we want to try to get to the essential points. Have you finished, Mr. Nobilo? I didn't mean to interrupt you. Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I had just finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn to my colleague. He has no questions. I have no questions either. Mr. Strukar, the Tribunal is very grateful to you for having come to The Hague to answer questions as best you can about difficult events and which are now rather far away in time, but you will now be able to go home. Please don't move for a moment. We're going to suspend the hearing, and we will resume in a half hour. There will be a Status Conference in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 3.55 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 15th day of January, 1999 at 9.45 a.m. 24 25
